title: Horsehead Nebula (NIRCam image)
caption: The Horsehead Nebula, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: Horsehead Nebula · constellation Orion · about 1300 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Webb, NASA, CSA, K. Misselt (University of Arizona) and A. Abergel (IAS/University Paris-Saclay, CNRS)

recognition.text: Ranked #73 on ESA/Webb’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Along the bottom of this view curves a wall of dense, smoky dust and gas, a close-up of the top of the Horsehead Nebula. Above it, distant stars and galaxies fill a background that fades from dark red to black, while one bright star throws six long spikes. These are the sharpest infrared images of the Horsehead to date.

Also called Barnard 33, the nebula lies roughly 1300 light-years away in Orion. It formed from a collapsing cloud and glows because a nearby hot star lights it. The surrounding gas has already dispersed, but the pillar's thick clumps resist erosion. Astronomers estimate it has about five million years left.

The Horsehead is a photon-dominated region, where ultraviolet light from massive stars heats a mostly neutral layer of gas and dust and drives its chemistry. Being close and almost edge-on, it is ideal for studying how radiation interacts with interstellar matter.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.13 x 2.14 arcminutes) and distance (1300 light years), the frame spans roughly 0.8 × 0.8 light-years. Its light set out about 1,300 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam. Shorter filters, including one for methane, are shown in blue. Water ice and molecular hydrogen appear in cyan, PAH molecules in green, carbon dioxide in orange, and molecular hydrogen and hydrogen's Brackett-alpha line in red.
understand.eye: This light is infrared and invisible to the eye, so the image translates chemistry and warmth into colors we can see.

explore: Such regions form where gas is dense enough to stay neutral but not so dense that far-ultraviolet light cannot get in. Their light helps astronomers trace how interstellar matter evolves, in our galaxy and across the history of the universe.
Webb's view sits in the western part of the Orion B molecular cloud.
alt: A curved wall of smoky gas and dust along the bottom, with distant stars and galaxies above and one bright star with six long spikes, against a background fading from dark red to black.
